systems.title: Sino-Korean and native Korean numbers
systems.goal: Say 일 to 십 the Sino-Korean way and 하나 to 열 the native Korean way. Read 0 as 영 and as 공, and learn where each set is used.

pastTen.title: Numbers bigger than ten
pastTen.goal: Build and read numbers past ten, and learn the five words that change shape when you count.

counting.title: Counting things
counting.goal: Count people, things and animals, say how old you are, and say the order.

time.title: What time? What date?
time.goal: Tell the time, and say the date and the day of the week.

money.title: How much? Which number?
money.goal: Read a price, a phone number and a floor, and read 만 원 and 억.

review.title: Mistakes people often make
review.goal: Check the five people get wrong most, then put it all together.

sinoBasics.title: Sino-Korean numbers: 일 to 십
sinoBasics.objective: Listen to 일, 이, 삼 up to 십, and say them after.
sinoBasics.step1: Numbers read 일, 이, 삼 are the Sino-Korean set. You use them for dates and months, minutes, prices and phone numbers.
sinoBasics.step2: Floors, addresses, measurements like length and weight, and any number past a hundred also take the Sino-Korean set.
sinoBasics.step3: 일 이 삼 사 오 육 칠 팔 구 십. Each one is a single syllable: 삼월 이일 · 오천 원 · 십 분 · 이 층 · 공일공.

nativeBasics.title: Native Korean numbers: 하나 to 열
nativeBasics.objective: Listen to 하나 up to 열, say them, and count things in front of you.
nativeBasics.step1: Numbers counted 하나, 둘, 셋 are the native Korean set. You use them to count things and people, to say an age, and for the hour on a clock.
nativeBasics.step2: 하나 둘 셋 넷 다섯 여섯 일곱 여덟 아홉 열. 여덟 is said 여덜. From a hundred up you count everything the Sino-Korean way.
nativeBasics.step3: Before a counting word the shape changes: 하나 → 한 개, 둘 → 두 개, 셋 → 세 개, 넷 → 네 개, 스물 → 스무 개.

zero.title: 0 is 영 or 공
zero.objective: Say 영 for an amount, and 공 when you read a number out.
zero.step1: 영 is zero as an amount — in maths, in a score, in a temperature below zero (영하).
zero.step2: 공 is the digit 0, read aloud in a phone number, a room number, a code. 010 is 공일공, never 영일영.

choosing.title: Things take 하나, 둘 · prices take 일, 이
choosing.objective: Choose whether a situation takes Sino-Korean or native Korean numbers.
choosing.step1: To count what you can see, use the native Korean set: 세 명, 두 시, 스무 살.
choosing.step2: For prices, dates, minutes, phone numbers and floors, use the Sino-Korean set: 오천 원, 삼월 일일, 삼십 분.
choosing.step3: A clock time uses both. 세 시 삼십 분 — the hour is native Korean 세, the minutes are Sino-Korean 삼십.

sinoBuild.title: Counting to a thousand
sinoBuild.objective: Build and read numbers like 십일, 이십 and 삼십오.
sinoBuild.step1: Read the parts in order, left to right.
sinoBuild.step2: Watch 십육: it is written 십육 but said 심뉵. A ㄴ-sound appears in front of 육, and that turns 십 into 심.
sinoBuild.step3: 백 is a hundred and 천 is a thousand. There is no 일 in front of them — 백 원, not 일백 원.

nativeBuild.title: Saying 열하나, 스물, 서른
nativeBuild.objective: Say numbers past ten the native Korean way.
nativeBuild.step1: Add the units to 열, up to 열아홉. Said as one word.
nativeBuild.step2: Each ten has its own word — 스물, 서른, 마흔, 쉰.
nativeBuild.step3: 열여섯 is said 열려섣. The same rule as 심뉵: a ㄴ-sound appears in front of 여섯, and after ㄹ it becomes ㄹ.

forms.title: 한 개, 두 개 — the shape changes
forms.objective: When you count, 하나 becomes 한 and 둘 becomes 두. There are five to remember.
forms.step1: Five words change shape in front of a counting word. 하나 becomes 한, 둘 becomes 두, 셋 becomes 세, 넷 becomes 네, 스물 becomes 스무.
forms.step2: This is not a small difference in pronunciation. People say 두 사람, not 둘 사람.
forms.step3: The rest keep their shape: 다섯 명, 여섯 개, 열 마리. Only those five change.

counters.title: 명 for people, 개 for things, 마리 for animals
counters.objective: Count like 세 명, 두 개 and 고양이 두 마리.
counters.step1: Korean never counts a noun with a number alone. Between the number and the thing there is a counting word, chosen by the kind of thing.
counters.step2: 명 counts people (세 명), 개 counts objects (두 개), 마리 counts animals (고양이 두 마리). 사람 also counts people, a little less formally.
counters.step3: The noun comes first, then the number and the counting word: 고양이 두 마리, not 두 마리 고양이.

countersEveryday.title: Two coffees, please
countersEveryday.objective: Order and count in a shop with 병, 잔, 장 and 권.
countersEveryday.step1: 병 is a bottle (맥주 한 병), 잔 is a cup or glass (커피 두 잔), 장 is a flat thing such as a ticket or a sheet (표 네 장), 권 is a book (책 세 권).
countersEveryday.step2: All four take the native Korean counting forms: 한 병, 두 잔, 세 권, 네 장.

age.title: How old are you?
age.objective: Say your age with 살, and ask an elder politely with 연세.
age.step1: 살 goes with the native Korean set: 스무 살, 스물다섯 살. 몇 살이에요? is what you ask a friend.
age.step2: 세 goes with the Sino-Korean set and you see it on forms and in the news: 이십 세.
age.step3: 살 is too casual for someone older. Ask an adult you have just met 나이가 어떻게 되세요?, and someone much older 연세가 어떻게 되세요? — 연세 is the honorific word for age.

ordinals.title: 첫 번째, 두 번째 — saying the order
ordinals.objective: Say where something comes in a line with 번째, and count off points with 첫째.
ordinals.step1: How many is one question; which one is another. 사과 두 개 is two apples. 두 번째 사과 is the second apple in the row.
ordinals.step2: Before 번째 use 첫, 두, 세, 네: 첫 번째, 두 번째, 세 번째, 네 번째. There is no 한 번째 and no 일 번째.
ordinals.step3: 첫째, 둘째 and 셋째 are one word, with no space. You use them to count off points: 첫째, 값이 싸요. 둘째, 가까워요.
ordinals.step4: For a place in a line, say 첫 번째, 두 번째. Keep 첫째, 둘째 for listing points and for which child in a family: 우리 집 둘째예요.

hours.title: What time is it?
hours.objective: Say the hour like 한 시 and 두 시, and use 반 for half past.
hours.step1: 시 takes the native Korean set: 한 시, 두 시, 세 시, 네 시, 열 시. 몇 시예요? asks the time.
hours.step2: 반 means half: 두 시 반 is half past two. It replaces 삼십 분.
hours.step3: Ask 몇 시예요? and answer like 세 시예요. Minutes come in the next lesson.

minutes.title: It's 3:30
minutes.objective: Say minutes and seconds, and join them to the hour.
minutes.step1: 분 and 초 take the Sino-Korean set: 삼십 분, 십오 분, 십 초.
minutes.step2: 세 시 삼십 분 — the hour is 세, the minutes are 삼십.
minutes.step3: Not 삼 시 서른 분. 세 시 삼십 분 is right.

dates.title: When is your birthday?
dates.objective: Say a date with 년, 월 and 일 — and watch out for 유월 and 시월.
dates.step1: 년, 월 and 일 are all Sino-Korean: 이천이십육년 삼월 십오일. Say the biggest unit first.
dates.step2: Two months are irregular. June is 유월, not 육월; October is 시월, not 십월.
dates.step3: 일 as a day of the month is the same word as 일 for one. 삼월 일일 is the first of March.

weekdays.title: What day is it today?
weekdays.objective: Say 월요일 to 일요일, and ask what day it is.
weekdays.step1: The days end in 요일: 월요일 Monday, 화요일, 수요일, 목요일, 금요일 Friday, 토요일, 일요일.
weekdays.step2: 무슨 요일이에요? asks what day it is. 주말 is the weekend.

money.title: How much is it?
money.objective: Read prices like 오천 원 and 만 오천 원.
money.step1: 원 takes the Sino-Korean set: 천 원, 오천 원. 얼마예요? asks the price.
money.step2: 만 원 is 10,000원. 삼만 오천 원 is 35,000원.
money.step3: 만 오천 원 is 15,000원 — one 만 and five 천.

digits.title: Reading a phone number
digits.objective: Read a number one digit at a time, saying 공 for 0 — floors and room numbers too.
digits.step1: A number you read out goes one digit at a time. 010 is 공일공.
digits.step2: 에 goes where a dash goes: 공일공에 일이삼사에 오륙칠팔.
digits.step3: Floors, room numbers and bus numbers take the Sino-Korean set: 삼 층, 오공이 호, 이백육 번 버스.

large.title: 만 원, 억 — reading big prices
large.objective: Read prices like 만 원 and 삼억 원, and read percentages and decimals.
large.step1: 만 is 10,000. 만 원 is the note in your wallet.
large.step2: 억 is 100,000,000. You hear it in flat prices and salaries: 삼억 원.
large.step3: Percentages are 오십 퍼센트, and the decimal point is 점: 삼 점 오 is 3.5.

pitfalls.title: Five things people often get wrong
pitfalls.objective: Spot and fix the five that trip people up.
pitfalls.step1: Each of these is a rule you have already met, in the place where it is easiest to forget.
pitfalls.step2: 두 살, not 둘 살. 십육 is said 심뉵. 유월, not 육월. 세 시 for the hour and 삼십 분 for the minutes. A space before the counting word.

mixed.title: Everything, mixed together
mixed.objective: Listen to and read what you have learned, all together.
mixed.step1: Everything so far, in one place. Things, hours and ages are native Korean; prices, minutes, dates and phone numbers are Sino-Korean.
mixed.step2: Read or listen, then choose. Looking at the explanation again is fine.

note.phoneZero: In a phone number, 0 is usually read 공.
note.countingForm: Before a counting word, 하나 becomes 한 and 둘 becomes 두.
note.irregularMonths: 6월 is read 유월 and 10월 is read 시월.
note.clockTime: A time is said like 세 시 십 분.
note.price: A price is said like 오천 원.
note.ordinalCounting: Before 번째 the number is 첫, 두, 세 or 네.
note.firstOrdinal: 첫 is its own word for the first one — not 하나 and not 한.
note.ordinalPoint: 첫째 and 둘째 open the points of what you are saying, one after another.
